facts.name_origin: From the Otoe-Missouria words Ni Brathge and the Omaha words Ní Btháska, both meaning 'flat water,' for the wide, slow Platte River.

government.chambers: One chamber only: 49 senators, each serving a 4-year term. Nebraska has the only unicameral (one-house) legislature in the country, and it is nonpartisan, so party names are not listed on the ballot. Voters chose this system in 1934, and it began in 1937.
government.executive: Governor (4-year term; cannot serve more than two terms in a row), who leads the executive branch along with the lieutenant governor, secretary of state, auditor of public accounts, state treasurer, and attorney general.
government.courts: Nebraska Supreme Court (seven judges: a chief justice and six associate justices, each representing one of six districts), chosen through a judicial nominating commission and appointed by the governor.
government.constitution: Current constitution written in 1875, one of the oldest state constitutions still in use; it has been amended more than 230 times. Nebraska's first constitution (1866) allowed only white men to vote, which delayed statehood until the wording was changed.
government.kid_line: "All persons are by nature free and independent, and have certain inherent and inalienable rights" (Nebraska Constitution, Article I, Section 1)

long_ago.about: One of the largest Plains nations, with ten thousand or more people, living along rivers in central Nebraska and northern Kansas. In spring women planted corn, beans, and squash near villages of dome-shaped earth lodges; in June whole villages traveled west to hunt bison for nearly three months.

The Omaha and Ponca once lived together east of the Mississippi River and moved west before 1500. By 1789 the Ponca had separated from the Omaha and lived where the Niobrara River flows into the Missouri. The Omaha built sturdy homes covered with sod.

Related nations who left the Great Lakes region in the 1500s and settled in the lower Missouri River valley. They traded with the Spanish, French, and Americans, and in 1804 they were the first nations to hold council with Lewis and Clark.

Branches of the Lakota were among the historic nations of western Nebraska. Chief Red Cloud of the Oglala Lakota came to the Niobrara River at Agate, and the Cook Collection of Lakota objects there includes a shirt decorated with quillwork that Red Cloud wore.

today.about: Reservation in northeastern Nebraska; about 5,400 enrolled members, including the community of Macy.
Reservation in northeastern Nebraska; about 4,200 enrolled members.
Reservation in northeastern Nebraska; about 2,600 enrolled members.
Has no reservation; its Service Delivery Area covers fifteen counties in Nebraska, Iowa, and South Dakota, set up by the Ponca Restoration Act.

first_peoples.today_note: The Pawnee gave up their Nebraska reservation in 1874 and moved to Oklahoma, where the Pawnee Nation is today. The Otoe-Missouria were moved to Red Rock, Oklahoma, in 1881. Many Ponca who were forced south in 1877 stayed in Oklahoma (the Southern Ponca), while Standing Bear's followers returned to their Niobrara homeland (the Northern, or Nebraska, Ponca).
sites: Pike-Pawnee Village Site near Guide Rock, a National Historic Landmark: a Republican Pawnee village of at least 102 earth lodges, lived in from about 1775 to 1830.
Agate Fossil Beds National Monument, which displays the Cook Collection of Lakota objects, including a quilled shirt worn by Red Cloud.
Scotts Bluff National Monument, which rises 800 feet above the North Platte River and was a landmark for Native peoples and later for travelers on the Oregon, California, and Mormon trails.

history.event: The Omaha and Ponca, who share a Siouan language, leave their home east of the Mississippi River and move west, later settling along the Missouri River.
The Otoe and Missouria separate from related nations in the Great Lakes region and move to the lower Missouri River valley.
A Spanish army expedition led by Pedro de Villasur is attacked and destroyed near today's Columbus by Pawnee and Otoe warriors who were allied with France. Spain stops exploring the area.
The Otoe and Missouria are the first nations to hold council with Lewis and Clark, who offer peace while claiming U.S. control over the land.
Lieutenant Zebulon Pike visits a Republican Pawnee village on the Republican River, days after Spanish soldiers had come with gifts. Spain and the United States were competing for Pawnee friendship.

The Kansas-Nebraska Act creates Nebraska Territory and lets territorial lawmakers decide whether to allow slavery. A few settlers from the South bring enslaved people: about 13 in 1855, and the 1860 census counted 15, most of them in Otoe County, around Nebraska City.

Freedom seekers escape from enslavers in Nebraska City. The nearby Mayhew Cabin, owned by Allen and Barbara (Kagi) Mayhew, becomes a stop on the Underground Railroad through the work of Barbara's brother John Kagi, who worked with abolitionist John Brown.
The territorial legislature votes to ban slavery. The governor vetoes the ban, but lawmakers override his veto and slavery is forbidden in Nebraska.
During the Civil War, no battles are fought in Nebraska Territory, but it raises three cavalry regiments for the Union, and more than 3,000 Nebraskans serve.
The Homestead Act offers 160 acres of free land to claimants, including families, immigrants, single women, and formerly enslaved people. Thousands settle on land long lived on by Native nations.

Nebraska becomes the 37th state on March 1. Its 1866 constitution let only white men vote, and that clause delayed statehood until lawmakers changed it. The capital moves from Omaha to Lancaster, renamed Lincoln.
Under heavy pressure from settlers, disease, and enemies, the Pawnee give up their Nebraska reservation and, over three years, move to Oklahoma.
The U.S. government forces the Ponca from their Niobrara homeland to Indian Territory (Oklahoma). Nine people die on the journey, including Standing Bear's daughter, Prairie Flower.
Standing Bear returns to bury his son and is arrested. In a trial in Omaha, Judge Elmer Dundy rules that 'an Indian is a person within the meaning of the law,' and Standing Bear is freed.

trailblazers.name: Standing Bear (Ma-chu-nah-zah)
trailblazers.text: After the U.S. forced the Ponca to Oklahoma, Standing Bear traveled home to Nebraska to keep a promise to bury his son by the Niobrara River. He was arrested, and in an 1879 federal trial in Omaha he spoke for his people. The judge ruled that a Native American is a person under the law, a landmark civil rights decision.

trailblazers.name: Susan La Flesche Picotte
trailblazers.text: Born on the Omaha Reservation, she graduated first in her class from the Woman's Medical College of Pennsylvania and became the first American Indian to receive a medical degree. At 24 she returned home as the only doctor for more than 1,200 people across 400 miles. In 1913 she opened a hospital in Walthill, the first on a reservation not funded by the government.

trailblazers.name: Mildred Brown
trailblazers.text: Mildred Brown helped start the Omaha Star newspaper in 1938 and later ran it on her own. The paper shared positive news of Omaha's Black community, refused ads from businesses that would not hire Black workers, and gave civil rights activists a place to meet.

trailblazers.name: Malcolm X (El-Hajj Malik el-Shabazz)
trailblazers.text: Born Malcolm Little in Omaha on May 19, 1925, to parents who led a local group working for Black independence, his family left Omaha to escape harassment and violence. He grew up to be a powerful voice for Black dignity and human rights. In 2022 he became the first Black person voted into the Nebraska Hall of Fame.

trailblazers.name: Ben Kuroki
trailblazers.years: 1917–2015 (he later gave his birth year as 1918)
trailblazers.text: Born in Gothenburg, Nebraska, Ben Kuroki grew up in Hershey, where his Japanese immigrant family grew vegetables to sell in North Platte. After Pearl Harbor he joined the Army Air Forces and faced racism and loneliness as the only Japanese American in his unit. He flew 58 combat missions over Europe and the Pacific, and in 1944 he visited three Japanese American incarceration camps.

landforms: Dissected Till Plains in the east, gently rolling hills left by Ice Age glaciers
Great Plains across most of the west
Sandhills, one of the largest grass-covered sand dune regions in the world
Pine Ridge and Wildcat Hills in the west
Scotts Bluff, rising 800 feet above the North Platte River
Panorama Point, the highest point (5,424 feet)
waters: Platte River, formed by the North Platte and South Platte
Niobrara River, a National Scenic River with more than 230 waterfalls
Huge underground aquifers: their water would stand 37.9 feet deep if spread over the whole state
geography.regions: Nebraska has two major land regions: the Dissected Till Plains in the east, where Omaha and Lincoln are, and the Great Plains in the west, which include the Sandhills, Pine Ridge, Rainwater Basin, High Plains, and Wildcat Hills.

ecosystems.name: Sandhills prairie
ecosystems.about: Grass holds the dunes in place. Crescent Lake National Wildlife Refuge, in the largest continuous sand dune area in the United States, protects wetlands and meadows where animals like the burrowing owl live.

ecosystems.name: Platte River
ecosystems.about: Each spring, from early March to mid-April, hundreds of thousands of sandhill cranes stop along the Platte to rest and feed during their migration.

ecosystems.name: Niobrara River Valley
ecosystems.about: Six kinds of ecosystems meet here, from northern forest to tallgrass prairie, and about 160 plant and animal species live at the very edge of their ranges.

science.weather: Nebraska is in Tornado Alley. Thunderstorms are common in spring and summer, and violent storms and tornadoes happen mostly in those seasons. Temperatures swing widely: the record high is 118°F (Minden, 1936) and the record low is -47°F (Camp Clarke, 1899).
science.resources: Agriculture drives the economy: farms and ranches cover 44 million acres, and 1 in 4 jobs are tied to agriculture. Top products are cattle and calves, corn, and soybeans, and Nebraska ranks first in the nation in beef exports.
science.highlight: Ashfall Fossil Beds: about 12 million years ago a volcanic eruption dropped ash on a watering hole near today's Royal, Nebraska. Over 200 complete fossil skeletons are preserved there, and visitors can watch scientists dig in the Hubbard Rhino Barn.

g3_ss.title: Nebraska's Communities and Government
g3_ss.plan: Locate Lincoln, Omaha, and tribal lands; learn how Nebraska's one-house, nonpartisan Unicameral makes laws and what the Governor and Supreme Court do.

g3_ss.title: Nebraska's First Peoples
g3_ss.plan: Explore Pawnee earth-lodge villages and the planting-and-hunting year, and meet the Omaha, Ponca, Winnebago, and Santee nations in Nebraska today.

g3_ss.title: Nebraska Trailblazers
g3_ss.plan: Story cards for Standing Bear, Susan La Flesche Picotte, Mildred Brown, Malcolm X, and Ben Kuroki; students explain how each stood up for fairness.

g45_ss.title: Nebraska's First Nations
g45_ss.plan: Compare Pawnee, Omaha and Ponca, Otoe-Missouria, and Lakota homelands and ways of life; read the meaning of 'Ni Brathge' and map the Platte.

g45_ss.title: Empires, Explorers, and the Territory
g45_ss.plan: The 1720 Villasur expedition, Lewis and Clark's council with the Otoe and Missouria, Pike at the Pawnee village, and the Kansas-Nebraska Act.

g45_ss.title: Slavery, Statehood, and Removal, 1854–1879
g45_ss.plan: Enslaved people and freedom seekers in Nebraska City, the Mayhew Cabin, the 1861 ban, the Civil War, homesteading, the 1866 voting clause and 1867 statehood, Pawnee and Ponca removal, and the Standing Bear trial.

g3_sci.title: Sandhill Crane Migration
g3_sci.plan: Why cranes stop on the Platte River every spring; track migration on a map and build a food-and-water habitat model.

g3_sci.title: Sand Dunes Held by Grass
g3_sci.plan: Test how grass roots keep sand from blowing away and connect it to the Sandhills and burrowing owls.

g3_sci.title: Fossils in Ash
g3_sci.plan: Ashfall Fossil Beds: how volcanic ash buried animals 12 million years ago and how scientists dig fossils carefully.

g45_sci.title: Tornado Alley
g45_sci.plan: How warm and cold air masses meet over Nebraska to form thunderstorms and tornadoes, plus tornado safety plans.

g45_sci.title: Water Under Our Feet
g45_sci.plan: Aquifers and irrigation: model groundwater with layers of gravel and sand, and discuss why farms depend on it.

g45_sci.title: Where Ecosystems Meet: the Niobrara
g45_sci.plan: Investigate how the 100th meridian and the Niobrara Valley mix eastern forests, western pines, and prairie; map species at the edge of their ranges.
